title: Flow
description: One network connection the sensor observed leaving the machine. A declared egress point says the code can reach a provider and an event says it did; a flow says bytes left, whether or not anything in the code explains them.
$comment: Metadata only. There is no field for payload bytes and none will be added: the sensor sees destinations, not contents, and the moment it could record contents it would become the leak it was deployed to find.

host_id.description: Machine the sensor ran on. Not a hostname: a stable opaque id, so a report does not carry infrastructure naming.

netns.description: Network namespace, so container traffic is not confused with host traffic.

t_start_bucket.description: Observation start, rounded to a fixed bucket. A raw microsecond stamp would put wall clock into an identity that has to compare equal across runs.

duration_ms.description: How long the connection was observed. There is no t_end_bucket: the end is t_start_bucket plus this, and two independently written fields for one fact can disagree with nothing to say which is right. Absent means the end was not observed, which is a fact rather than a zero.

five_tuple.description: The connection key. There is no src_ip: it names the machine rather than the connection, and it moves under DHCP, NAT and container restarts, so the same connection would hash to two flow ids across two runs. host_id and netns carry what it was standing in for.

proto.description: The IP protocol, which is the only thing the tuple can name. QUIC is carried over UDP; a tuple that read quic for one observation of a connection and udp for another would give that connection two identities.

interface.description: Interface the connection was seen on. Optional because a record seeded from a socket table snapshot has no interface to report, and a required field the sensor cannot fill makes it drop the record or invent a value. A utun name is the reason this is worth carrying: it says the traffic went through a tunnel.

resolved_host.description: Destination name, when one could be established.

resolved_host_source.description: How the name was established. Reported because the two sources can disagree and a reader needs to know which one produced this. dns_and_sni is corroboration, and its opposite is the dns_sni_mismatch degradation.

sni.description: Server name as the handshake presented it. Present only when sni_source is client_hello: under an encrypted or absent ClientHello there is no name to record, and a value here would contradict the field that says so.

sni_source.description: Required. encrypted_client_hello means the name is genuinely unavailable rather than merely missing, and the two must not read alike.

dns_names.description: Names the observed DNS answers mapped to this destination, lexicographically ascending. Carried because degraded_reasons can say dns_sni_mismatch, and without this the record states a disagreement while showing only one side of it.

classification.description: Whether the destination could be resolved and named. This is the distinction provider_ref cannot carry: unclassified and opaque both write provider_ref unknown, and only this field separates we looked at a name and no signature matched from there was never a name to look at. The second is a measured blind spot and the report's most important line.

provider_confidence.description: How the provider was established. A signature matched on a host name is a structural fact; a match on an address range is a guess, and the project forbids a guess from reaching the confirmed list. Present only when classification is classified: a confidence about a classification that does not exist is a claim about nothing.

ruleset_version.description: Version of the signature set that produced the classification, for the same reason a finding names detector.rule_version: a classification nobody can trace back to a rule set cannot be explained or reproduced. Present only when classification is classified.

process_attribution.description: How the owning process was determined. Kernel context is certain; an inference from a socket table snapshot is not, and a flow nobody could attribute is still reported.

pid_start_time.description: Guards against pid reuse: a pid alone can name two different processes over a long observation.

flow_scope.description: Which bucket this flow falls into. Only in_scope can produce an unmatched traffic finding. The other three never enter false positive accounting and are never hidden either: a bucket that disappears from the report is a silent swallow, which is what the counting was meant to prevent.

degraded_reasons.description: pre_existing_connection means bytes_out and duration_ms are lower bounds and t_start_bucket is when observation began, not when the connection did. A threshold rule must not discard such a record for falling under a limit.

allOf.$comment: A server name can only exist where the handshake showed one. Recording a name alongside encrypted_client_hello or absent would contradict the field that measures the blind spot, and the contradiction would read as data.

Provider confidence and rule set version describe a classification. Carrying them on a record that classified nothing would attach a confidence to a claim nobody made. The reverse is deliberately not required: a build whose classifier has not run yet still reports its flows, and a required field it cannot fill would make it drop them instead.
